questions.cardText:
[Zoology] What unusual physical behavior do rats exhibit when happy?
A. Their tails curl
B. Their whiskers cease to move
C. Their eyes bulge in and out
Answer: C. When rats are happy, they exhibit a behavior known as “eye boggling,” where their eyes rhythmically bulge in and out due to rapid movement of the jaw muscles.
questions.de: Wie heißt das Verhalten, bei dem die Augen einer zufriedenen Ratte durch die Bewegung ihrer Kiefermuskeln beim Zähneknirschen schnell hervortreten und wieder zurückgehen?
questions.en: What is the name of the behavior in which a contented rat's eyes rapidly bulge in and out, caused by the movement of its jaw muscles while it grinds its teeth?

timeline.labelEn: John Berkenhout gives the brown rat its scientific name (Mus norvegicus)
timeline.labelDe: John Berkenhout gibt der Wanderratte ihren wissenschaftlichen Namen (Mus norvegicus)

questions.notes: Card confirmed: Wikipedia ties boggling to vigorous bruxing (teeth grinding), most usually triggered by happiness; the eyes bulge because the lower-jaw muscles move behind the eye socket. German has no established term; the English term is given.

questions.cardText:
[Ecology] Which of the following is true about the impact that global climate change has on wine production?
A. Causes grapes to ripen too quickly, affecting the wine’s flavor
B. Causes a decrease in wine’s alcohol content
C. Causes grapes to ripen too slowly, leading to underproduction of grapes
Answer: A.
questions.de: Wie hat die globale Erwärmung seit den 1980er-Jahren den Zeitpunkt der Traubenreife in den meisten Weinregionen der Welt verändert?
questions.en: How has global warming changed the timing of grape ripening in most of the world's wine regions since the 1980s?

timeline.labelEn: Harvest records show grapes ripening earlier in most of the world's wine regions
timeline.labelDe: Lesedaten zeigen, dass Trauben in den meisten Weinregionen der Welt früher reifen

source.title: How will climate change affect wine?

questions.notes: Card answer A broadly right: harvest records show earlier ripening since the 1980s; warmer ripening means more sugar (so HIGHER alcohol, the opposite of option B) and lower acidity. The Connexion article notes growers can offset this by picking earlier.
